purpose: How a website-and-hosting reseller runs a portfolio of launched small-business sites as a recurring-revenue book: where the sites live and how one site's failure is contained, how backups, restores, updates, security, monitoring and incidents are operated and proven rather than asserted, how care tiers are built to promise only what operations can actually deliver and are repriced from measured cost-to-serve, how monthly reporting and the yearly review make invisible work visible using only evidence a client can inspect, and how accounts are retained, recovered from payment failure, reactivated or gracefully offboarded with a complete client-owned asset handover instead of lock-in.
assumptions: no observed dataset supplied; all scores are heuristic priors

the operator is a solo or very small website-and-hosting reseller carrying a portfolio of small marketing sites, with support capacity measured in one person's available hours rather than a team roster
sites arrive from the delivery pipeline already launched, with a runbook, a client-owned domain and delegated access in place; care operations receive and run them rather than build them
hosting is resold or rented from an upstream vendor rather than owned hardware, so the operator controls configuration, process and communication but not the underlying platform's uptime

all money content is mechanism only - tier contents, cost-to-serve derivation, repricing protocol and qualitative bands; actual amounts come from the operator's own invoices, logged minutes and live local quote checks, never from remembered or assumed market rates

privacy, breach-notification, consumer-contract and cancellation-notice obligations differ by jurisdiction and change over time; this KB names the obligation class and defers every specific to current rules verified where the operator and the client each operate
the client owns their domain, content, data and site files at every moment of the relationship, including during a billing dispute and during offboarding
exclusions: productizing and pricing the site-build-plus-care offer, niche selection, referral acquisition, pre-sale discovery, scope agreement and expectation-setting before signature - the productized web offer and client acquisition KB owns those

choosing the build stack, running the build pipeline (content intake, design system, build, staging review), the launch-time quality, performance and accessibility baseline, and the domain, DNS and email cutover itself - the site build and delivery KB owns those

invented market rates, firm monthly prices, margin percentages or account-value multiples stated as fact - care-plan money appears here only as tier mechanisms, cost-to-serve derivation from the operator's own records, and qualitative bands
SEO, traffic, ranking, lead-volume or revenue guarantees of any kind, and any uptime or performance claim the operator cannot show the client the underlying measurement for

any retention or collections tactic that relies on holding the client's domain, content, database, backups or credentials as leverage - assets stay client-owned and the exit path stays open even during a billing dispute

personalized legal, tax, insurance or financial advice - privacy, breach-notification, consumer-protection and contract points are named as obligation classes to verify under current rules in the relevant jurisdiction, with the client referred to their own advisers
operating the client's third-party vendor accounts on their behalf (booking, payments, review platforms, ad accounts) and campaign work such as advertising, content marketing or link building

competency_questions.question: What does the care operation promise to do for every site under management, and what does it explicitly refuse to promise?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: CARE_OPERATIONS_CHARTER states the scheduled work, the on-request work, the out-of-scope work and the overriding principles, and PERFORMANCE_CLAIM_INTEGRITY states the classes of claim that are never made

competency_questions.question: Where should a portfolio of small client sites actually live, and how does that choice change blast radius, cost per site, and the ability to move one site out later?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: HOSTING_PLATFORM_ARCHITECTURE gives the tenancy and isolation decision with its cost and portability consequences, and HOST_VENDOR_DEPENDENCY_AND_EXIT gives the supplier-risk and rehearsed-migration answer

competency_questions.question: Who owns which account behind each client's site, and how is that recorded so any client could leave next week with everything intact?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: ACCOUNT_OWNERSHIP_REGISTER defines the per-client account inventory, the ownership rule for client assets, and the delegated-access model that can be revoked without breaking the site

competency_questions.question: What must be true about a newly launched site before it is allowed to start billing as a care client?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: CARE_ENROLLMENT_INTAKE lists the verified backup and restore point, working delegated access, monitoring in place, recorded expiries, recorded tier inclusions and confirmed billing terms as enrollment conditions

competency_questions.question: How are backups designed and proven so that 'we have backups' is a fact rather than an assumption?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: BACKUP_REGIME_DESIGN derives scope, frequency, off-account copy and retention from change rate and tolerable loss, and RESTORE_DRILL_PROOF supplies the timed restore evidence

competency_questions.question: How do you update platform and extensions across a whole portfolio without breaking client sites, and what happens when a site's platform reaches end of life?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: UPDATE_CYCLE_OPERATIONS defines the restore-point-first batched window, the security-patch exception, the post-update check and rollback, and the tech-debt escalation path to a rebuild conversation

competency_questions.question: What ongoing security work is honestly included, how is trouble detected, and what is done the morning a client's site is defaced, unreachable or blacklisted?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SECURITY_MAINTENANCE_BASELINE states the hygiene set and its likelihood-reduction framing, MONITORING_AND_EXPIRY_WATCH states what is watched and how alerts route, and INCIDENT_RESPONSE_AND_RECOVERY gives the confirm-contain-notify-restore-close sequence

competency_questions.question: What obligations follow from holding other people's personal data in form submissions, site databases and every backup copy of them?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: DATA_PROTECTION_OBLIGATIONS names the obligation class, the data map across live and backup copies, the retention-versus-deletion rule, and the instruction to verify current rules in the applicable jurisdictions rather than assert specifics

competency_questions.question: How are care tiers built so that each tier promises only what operations can actually deliver, and what belongs to every site regardless of tier?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: CARE_TIER_ARCHITECTURE derives tier contents from existing timed procedures, forbids unlimited human work, and names the floor obligations that are never gated behind a higher tier

competency_questions.question: What counts as an included edit, how are requests taken in and answered, and how does a project-sized request become a quote instead of an argument?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: EDIT_ALLOWANCE_AND_PROJECT_BOUNDARY defines the request unit, the included and excluded lists, the rollover rule and the quote trigger, and SUPPORT_INTAKE_AND_RESPONSE_PROMISE defines the single logged channel, the triage classes and the response windows

competency_questions.question: What does one site actually cost to keep every month, and how is a price change decided, communicated and applied fairly?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: COST_TO_SERVE_AND_REPRICING derives per-client cost from the operator's own invoices and logged minutes and states the fix-rescope-reprice ladder with advance written notice and a lower-tier or clean-exit alternative

competency_questions.question: What goes into the monthly report and the yearly review so the client can see the value, without being told anything that cannot be evidenced?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: VALUE_REPORTING_CADENCE lists the report contents traceable to records plus the periodic review conversation, and PERFORMANCE_CLAIM_INTEGRITY supplies the rules that keep every reported number verifiable and guarantee-free

competency_questions.question: Which signals say an account is about to cancel, which retention responses are legitimate rather than manipulative, and how is a failed payment handled with dignity?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: CHURN_SIGNAL_TRIAGE lists the leading signals with a diagnose-before-discount rule, ETHICAL_RETENTION_GUARDRAILS states the no-fear-selling, disclosure-first, easy-cancellation and vulnerable-client constraints, and PAYMENT_FAILURE_AND_DUNNING gives the retry, notice and suspension ladder that never touches client-owned assets

competency_questions.question: How many sites can one operator carry, when should an account be repriced, right-sized or released, and what exactly is handed over when a client leaves or comes back?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PORTFOLIO_CAPACITY_AND_BOOK_REVIEW ties enrollment limits to recurring hours plus incident reserve and produces one decision per account, OFFBOARDING_ASSET_HANDOVER specifies the complete handover pack and timeline, and LAPSED_CLIENT_REACTIVATION specifies the honest re-entry assessment

glossary.definition: The recurring monthly service sold alongside a site build: custody of the hosting arrangement plus a named set of scheduled work (backups, updates, monitoring, reporting) and on-request work (a bounded edit allowance, support within a stated response window). It is a service subscription, not a licence to use the site - the site itself belongs to the client whether or not the plan continues.

A hosting plan bought by the operator that can hold many client sites under one supplier relationship and one invoice. It lowers cost per site and centralizes administration, but concentrates supplier risk and can widen the blast radius unless each site is isolated inside it.

How many clients are affected when one thing goes wrong - a compromised site, a suspended account, an exhausted resource limit, a supplier outage. Architecture decisions in this subdomain are largely blast-radius decisions traded against cost per site.

A rehearsed restoration of a real site's backup into a scratch location, walked through and timed, to convert the claim 'backups exist' into the evidence 'this site was restored in this long, to this point in time, with these files and this database intact'.

Two separate promises: how much recent work a restore would lose (the age of the newest usable backup) and how long the site would be down while it is restored. Both are properties of the operator's actual regime and drill measurements, not of the word 'backup' on a price sheet.

What one client actually consumes per month: their share of hosting and backup storage, licences, monitoring and payment processing, plus the logged human minutes spent on their updates, checks, support, edits and reporting. Measured per client, because portfolio averages hide the accounts that consume the margin of ten others.

The sequence that follows a failed recurring payment: automatic retry, a plainly worded notice to a channel a human reads, an escalation ladder with stated dates, and suspension only per previously agreed terms - distinct from collections of a genuine debt and never involving the withholding of client-owned assets.

Accounts lost to payment mechanics rather than decisions - an expired card, a closed bank account, a changed billing email nobody monitors. It is usually recoverable by a well-timed human message and is the cheapest churn to prevent.

A content-management core, language runtime or extension that no longer receives security fixes from its maintainer. It cannot be made safe by continued patching, so it converts silently into portfolio tech debt with only two honest paths: an in-place upgrade that the site's customizations may block, or a rebuild proposed as a project.

The complete set a departing client receives: site files and database export, media library, a current backup they can hold, the DNS zone as it stands, the account inventory with instructions to take over each, the runbook, and any assets produced during the relationship - delivered on a stated timeline with the operator's delegated access removed afterwards and nothing withheld pending payment.

nodes.definition: Write down, before the first site is enrolled, exactly what the care operation does for every site under management and what it refuses to do: which work happens on a schedule without being asked (backups, update cycles, monitoring, monthly reporting), which work happens on request inside a stated response window, which work is explicitly out of scope and becomes a quoted project, and the standing principles that outrank commercial convenience - the client owns their domain, content and data at every moment; every claim made to a client must be traceable to a record the client could inspect; and no site is enrolled that the operation cannot actually serve at the promised level. This is an internal operating document rather than a sales page, and its purpose is single: the tiers, the intake checklist, the report template, the incident message and the offboarding pack are all derived from it, so what a client is told and what the operation does are the same thing.

included: the scheduled, on-request and out-of-scope work split
the three standing principles that override commercial pressure
the derivation source for tiers, checklists, reports and exit packs
excluded: the headline price and the sales narrative of the offer, which belong to the offer stage
per-site build decisions and the launch pipeline

pros.claim: A written promise set makes every downstream artifact consistent instead of improvised per client
pros.example: the tier sheet, the enrollment checklist and the monthly report all list the same four scheduled items, so a client comparing them finds no gaps

pros.claim: Stating what is refused up front removes the awkward monthly negotiation about work that was never included
pros.example: 'we do not run advertising campaigns or write your content' answered once in the charter, not re-argued in six separate email threads

cons.claim: A charter written before the operation has run is partly aspirational and will be contradicted by the first hard month
cons.example: a promise of same-day responses written in a quiet month and broken during the week two sites are compromised at once

failure_modes: leaving the promise set implicit so each client believes a slightly different version of the plan
writing the charter as marketing copy, which imports adjectives such as full-service and unlimited that operations then cannot honor
never revising it after operations prove one of its promises unrealistic
acceptance_tests: the charter names, for every site under management, the scheduled work, the on-request work with its response window, the out-of-scope list, and the three standing principles
each client-facing artifact - tier sheet, enrollment checklist, monthly report, incident message, exit pack - can be traced back to a line in the charter
revisit_triggers: a promise in the charter is missed twice in a quarter
capacity review shows the promise set cannot be met at current book size
a new class of work is being performed for clients that the charter does not mention

base.update_signal: operations repeatedly deliver something different from what the charter states, in either direction

nodes.definition: Decide where the portfolio physically lives and how one site's bad day is stopped from becoming everyone's bad day. The realistic options for a small reseller are one reseller or agency plan holding many sites, one hosting account per client paid for by the client, a managed platform billed per site, or a self-administered server; each moves three dials at once - cost per site, blast radius when a site is compromised, suspended or resource-starved, and how cleanly a single site can be exported and handed to a stranger. The same decision fixes who receives the supplier's invoice and control panel, which operational features come free from the platform (snapshots, staging, mail routing, certificate renewal) and which must be run by hand, and how sites are isolated from one another - separate account or container, separate database user, separate credentials - so a vulnerable form on one client's site cannot read another client's data. It is chosen once for the portfolio, revisited rarely, and every operational procedure downstream inherits its limits.

included: tenancy and isolation model across the portfolio
who holds each hosting account and receives the invoice
which operational capabilities come from the platform versus by hand
the per-site export requirement that keeps sites portable
excluded: launch-time DNS cutover and email continuity, which the delivery pipeline owns
the client's registrar choice and domain purchase
content-management platform and build-stack selection

pros.claim: An isolation-first layout keeps one compromised site from becoming a portfolio-wide incident
pros.example: an outdated form extension on a restaurant site is cleaned in an afternoon because it ran under its own account and database user, with no other client touched

pros.claim: Deciding the architecture once makes batch operations possible at all
pros.example: one update round covering every site because they all sit on the same platform with the same access pattern, instead of twenty different logins and habits

cons.claim: Isolation and per-client accounts raise cost per site and multiply the panels, invoices and renewal dates to administer
cons.example: twenty separate client-owned hosting accounts means twenty billing contacts and twenty renewal dates to track, several of which will lapse on a client's expired card

failure_modes: packing the entire book into one cheap shared account, so a single infection, resource limit or supplier suspension takes every client offline at once
choosing a platform whose only export is a proprietary snapshot no other host can restore, quietly creating the lock-in the business promised never to use
letting the architecture drift into a mix of one-off arrangements per client until no procedure applies to all sites
acceptance_tests: the architecture note states the tenancy model, the isolation boundary between sites, and the account holder and invoice recipient for each layer
one representative site has been exported from the platform and restored somewhere else, with the elapsed time and any missing pieces recorded
revisit_triggers: the supplier changes plan limits, pricing or terms
the portfolio approaches the plan's site, storage or resource ceilings
an incident crosses the boundary between two client sites

base.update_signal: a cross-site incident, a supplier limit change, or a failed export proves the tenancy model wrong

nodes.definition: Treat the upstream hosting supplier as a vendor that can fail, reprice, deprecate a plan or be acquired, and hold a rehearsed answer for each case. The work has four parts: reading what the supplier's own service commitment actually covers and excludes, so nothing is promised onward to clients that the supplier has not promised to the operator; inventorying which supplier features the portfolio has quietly become dependent on - their snapshot system, their caching layer, their staging tool, their mail relay, their certificate automation - and what replacing each would cost in hours; keeping a current, tested export of at least one representative site that has been restored on a different provider, so migration is a known procedure rather than a hope; and writing the trigger list that converts concentration risk into action - repeated outages, a price change that breaks the book's economics, a discontinued plan, or support quality that collapses. This is the difference between a reseller who has a supplier and a reseller who has a dependency with a story to tell clients.

included: what the supplier commitment covers and the limits on passing it through to clients
the dependency inventory with replacement cost in hours
a rehearsed migration of a representative site
written switch triggers
excluded: client-facing communication during a live outage, which the incident node owns
the client's own registrar and third-party vendor relationships
the initial tenancy decision itself

pros.claim: A rehearsed migration turns a supplier crisis from an existential event into a scheduled weekend of work
pros.example: a discontinued plan notice met with a migration path already timed on a test site, so clients hear a date rather than an apology

cons.claim: Portability discipline forfeits the deepest supplier conveniences and costs unbillable rehearsal time
cons.example: declining a one-click supplier optimization layer because nothing outside that supplier can restore what it produces

cons.claim: Second-guessing a supplier too often produces migration churn that is itself a source of client-visible breakage
cons.example: two host moves in one year, each carrying its own mail-routing surprise, spent on a problem the clients never felt

failure_modes: repeating the supplier's uptime language to clients as if the operator guaranteed it
discovering during an outage that nobody has ever restored a site outside the supplier's own control panel
having no written trigger, so a slowly worsening supplier is tolerated for years out of inertia
acceptance_tests: the dependency inventory names every supplier feature the portfolio relies on with an estimated replacement effort
a representative site has been restored with a different provider within the last review period and the elapsed time recorded
the switch trigger list exists in writing with the conditions that would start a migration
revisit_triggers: the supplier changes terms, pricing or ownership
an outage exceeds what the book can absorb without client compensation questions
a dependency is added, such as adopting the supplier's proprietary backup or caching product

base.update_signal: a supplier term, price or reliability change, or a migration rehearsal that takes far longer than assumed

nodes.definition: Maintain, per client, a register of every account the site depends on - registrar, DNS host, web host, mailbox provider, platform licences and paid extensions, form or booking vendor, analytics, payment gateway, content delivery or security service - and for each: whose legal name and payment card it sits under, which email address controls password recovery, what access the operator holds and by which mechanism (a delegated user, a shared vault entry, an agency or reseller relationship), and the renewal or expiry date. Two rules make the register more than a spreadsheet: the client's name is on the assets the client owns, above all the domain and the content, and the operator's access is delegated access that can be revoked without breaking anything. Kept current at enrollment and at every change, this register is simultaneously the skeleton of the exit pack, the contact list during an incident, and the standing proof that retention here is earned by service rather than secured by holding the keys.

included: the per-client account inventory with owner, recovery address, access mechanism and renewal date
the ownership rule separating client-owned assets from operator-owned tooling
revocable delegated access as the standing access model
excluded: the launch-time transfer of a domain into the client's name, which delivery performs
the sales-stage ownership promise and how it is positioned
storing credentials in the register itself rather than referencing the vault

pros.claim: A current register makes a clean exit or an emergency takeover a one-hour task instead of an archaeology project
pros.example: a client's bookkeeper asking who the registrar is and getting an accurate answer with the renewal date in the same reply

pros.claim: Recording ownership honestly removes the temptation to rely on control as retention
pros.example: a departing client's domain moves out on request because it was always in their name, and the relationship ends on good terms that later produce a referral

cons.claim: Client-owned accounts mean client-controlled failures the operator must chase but cannot fix directly
cons.example: a domain renewal charged to a card the client cancelled, discovered only because the register carried the date and someone chased it

failure_modes: accounts opened in the operator's name for convenience during a rush and never corrected, so the ownership promise is false in the ledger
recovery email addresses pointing at a mailbox nobody at the client reads any more
credentials pasted into the register itself rather than referenced from a vault, turning one document into the whole portfolio's risk
acceptance_tests: every enrolled site has a register entry naming owner, recovery address, access mechanism and renewal date for each account it depends on
for each client-owned asset the entry shows the client's name, and for each operator access the entry shows a revocable delegated mechanism rather than a shared personal password
revisit_triggers: any account is added, moved, renewed or closed
the client's staff or ownership changes
an access attempt fails because a recovery address or delegated user no longer works

base.update_signal: an exit, incident or renewal reveals an account whose true owner or recovery path differs from the register

nodes.definition: Run the receiving half of the launch handoff before the first monthly charge exists. The intake confirms that the runbook received from delivery matches reality (stack and extension versions, where the site is hosted, how mail leaves it, which forms route where), takes and verifies an independent first backup with its restore point recorded, puts monitoring on the site with alerts routed to a channel the operator watches, registers the domain, certificate and licence expiry dates in the calendar, proves the delegated access works by using it, writes the tier sold and its specific inclusions into the client record, confirms the billing instrument, billing date and the written cancellation and notice terms the client agreed to, and sets the date the first report will arrive. Anything missing is chased before enrollment rather than after, because a site that starts billing with an unverified backup, an unrecorded recovery address and a tier nobody wrote down is precisely the site that produces the late-night emergency and the 'what am I actually paying for' email seven months later.

included: runbook verification against the live site
first independent backup with a confirmed restore point
monitoring, alert routing and expiry registration
delegated access proven by use
tier inclusions, billing terms and reporting start recorded
excluded: the delivery-side definition-of-done that releases the site from the build pipeline
client training on editing their own site
designing the tier being enrolled into

pros.claim: A gate before the first charge stops silently unprotected sites from accumulating in the book
pros.example: intake catching that a site launched in a rush has backups switched off, before it starts billing as a protected site

pros.claim: Recording the exact inclusions at enrollment ends future disputes about what was sold
pros.example: a client asking in month nine whether their plan covers a new booking page, answered from their own record in one line

cons.claim: Intake friction delays recurring revenue when the client is slow to supply access or confirm billing
cons.example: a site live for three weeks but not enrolled because the owner has not shared registrar access or answered the billing confirmation

failure_modes: starting billing on a promise that the delivery handoff was complete rather than verifying it
accepting a runbook that describes the site as designed rather than as it actually launched
leaving cancellation and notice terms verbal, so the first exit becomes an argument about what was agreed
acceptance_tests: no site appears in billing without a completed intake record showing verified backup and restore point, working delegated access, active monitoring, registered expiries and written tier inclusions
the billing instrument, billing date and cancellation terms are recorded and were confirmed by the client in writing
revisit_triggers: the delivery handoff contents change
an incident traces back to something intake should have caught
the tier structure changes what has to be recorded at enrollment

base.update_signal: a post-enrollment surprise that a stricter intake item would have surfaced

nodes.definition: Define what is copied, how often, to where, and for how long, from the business reality of each site rather than from a default toggle. Scope covers site files, the database, uploaded media, the platform configuration and a written copy of the DNS zone, because a restore that returns the files but loses the mail records has not returned the business. Location requires at least one copy that does not live inside the hosting account it protects, since account suspension, supplier failure and a compromise that reaches the panel all destroy in-account copies. Frequency is derived: how often does this site's content change, and how much recent work could the owner tolerate losing - a shop taking orders daily and a tradesman whose text changed twice this year sit at opposite ends, and the tier's promise must match the schedule actually configured. Retention has to span the gap between an infection happening and someone noticing it, so that a clean generation still exists, while staying inside the deletion commitments the data-protection obligations impose. Access to backup storage is restricted and the copies encrypted, and a labelled restore point is taken immediately before any risky operation.

included: what is copied including configuration and the DNS zone
at least one copy outside the hosting account
frequency and retention derived from change rate, tolerable loss and detection lag
backup storage access control and encryption
pre-change restore points
excluded: proving a restore actually works, which is the drill node
the client's own copies of source material and photography
archival of the client's business records unrelated to the site

pros.claim: An off-account copy survives the failures that destroy in-panel snapshots
pros.example: a suspended hosting account taking its own snapshots with it while the external weekly copy restores the site elsewhere

pros.claim: Retention long enough to outlast detection lag preserves a clean generation to return to
pros.example: a compromise noticed three weeks after it began, recovered from the generation that predates the injected files

cons.claim: Depth costs storage and administration, and every generation kept is another copy of personal data to secure and eventually delete
cons.example: months of daily copies of a booking database, each holding customer contact details, on storage the operator pays for and must protect

failure_modes: trusting the supplier's default snapshots without knowing their frequency, retention or restore path
backing up files but not the database, or the database but not the uploads directory
keeping every copy inside the same account or provider that would be lost in the failure being insured against
setting one universal schedule that under-protects the busy site and over-stores the static one
acceptance_tests: for each site the regime states the scope, the frequency, the retention span and the off-account location, with the tolerable-loss reasoning recorded
the promised backup behaviour in the client's tier matches the schedule actually configured on that site
backup storage is access-restricted and encrypted, and retention is inside the deletion commitments in force
revisit_triggers: a restore drill fails or recovers less than expected
a site's change rate or business model shifts, such as adding online ordering
storage cost or a deletion obligation forces a retention change

base.update_signal: a drill or a real recovery shows the scope, frequency or retention did not cover the case that occurred

nodes.definition: Convert the claim that backups exist into the evidence that a site can be brought back. On a rotation that eventually touches every site in the portfolio, restore a real backup into a scratch location, time the whole operation from decision to working site, and walk the result: do the uploads exist, do the database references resolve, do the forms still send, do the certificates and credentials the site depends on still work outside the original account. Drills also run after any change to the backup system, the hosting plan or the platform. Three outputs matter: the measured recovery time, which is the only honest answer to a client asking how long they would be down; the observed recovery point, which is the only honest answer to how much work they would lose; and a defect list that feeds straight back into the backup regime. An operator who has never restored anything is running an untested insurance policy and quoting from imagination.

included: scheduled rotation of real restores into a scratch location
timing and walking the restored site
measured recovery time and recovery point as the source of client-facing statements
defect feedback into the backup regime
excluded: the live incident itself, which follows the incident playbook
load testing or performance benchmarking of the restored site
restoring a client's third-party vendor data such as their payment processor records

pros.claim: A timed drill replaces a guess with a number the operator can state and defend
pros.example: answering 'a full restore of your site took just under two hours the last time we rehearsed it, on this date' instead of 'it should be quick'

pros.claim: Drills surface the silent defects that only appear during restoration
pros.example: discovering that the media library lived outside the backup scope, found in a rehearsal rather than during an outage

cons.claim: Drills consume unbillable hours that always look postponable against paying work
cons.example: the quarterly rehearsal slipping three times in a row because build work filled the calendar

cons.claim: A drill in a scratch environment can still miss conditions that only exist in production
cons.example: a restore that works perfectly until it needs the mail relay credentials that only the live account holds

failure_modes: verifying only that a backup file exists rather than that it restores
restoring the files and declaring success without opening the site or testing a form
drilling one easy site repeatedly while the complex sites are never exercised
acceptance_tests: the drill log shows, per drill, the site, the date, the elapsed restore time, the recovery point achieved, and the defects found
every site in the portfolio has been exercised within the stated rotation period, and any client-facing recovery statement cites a real drill
revisit_triggers: a drill exceeds the recovery time the client was told to expect
the backup system, hosting plan or platform changes
a real incident recovery diverges from what drills predicted

base.update_signal: a drill or live recovery whose elapsed time or recovered state differs materially from the last recorded result

nodes.definition: Run platform, extension and theme updates across many sites on a rhythm that trades speed against safety deliberately rather than by accident. The cycle: a scheduled window per site or per batch; a labelled restore point taken immediately before touching anything; security-critical fixes broken out of the batch and applied ahead of schedule because a known exploited vulnerability does not wait for the calendar; updates applied to a staging copy first where the site's complexity or the tier justifies it; a post-update walk of the pages and functions that matter to that particular business - the booking form, the menu page, the checkout, the phone link - rather than a glance at the home page; and a recorded rollback when the walk fails. The cycle also owns aging: an abandoned extension, a platform version approaching end of life, or a customization that blocks updating is logged as portfolio tech debt with a named remediation path and escalated into a rebuild conversation, never silently skipped forever while the report keeps saying updates were applied.

included: scheduled batch windows with a pre-update restore point
security-patch fast path outside the batch
staging-first policy where complexity or tier warrants it
per-site functional walk after updating and recorded rollback
tech-debt and end-of-life logging with a remediation path
excluded: building new features or redesigns, which are quoted projects
the client's own content edits
the original build's stack choice

pros.claim: Batching with a restore point makes updates routine and cheap per site instead of individually risky
pros.example: one window covering the portfolio, with the single site that broke rolled back inside ten minutes because its restore point was minutes old

pros.claim: A functional walk catches the breakage that matters to that business rather than the breakage that is visually obvious
pros.example: noticing after an update that the contact form silently stopped delivering, before the client loses a week of enquiries

cons.claim: Batched windows mean a site can sit for days on a version with a known problem unless the security fast path is honored
cons.example: a widely exploited extension flaw disclosed the day after a window closed, forcing an out-of-cycle round across the whole portfolio

cons.claim: Staging-first doubles the handling cost per site and is disproportionate for a simple brochure site
cons.example: spinning up a staging copy of a five-page site to update two extensions that have never once broken it

failure_modes: updating with no restore point and no rollback path
skipping a site's updates indefinitely because a customization breaks and nobody logs the debt or tells the client
checking only that the home page loads and missing the broken form, booking widget or checkout
letting an end-of-life platform version quietly persist while reporting continues to claim the site is maintained
acceptance_tests: every update round records the site, what was updated, the restore point taken, the functional checks performed and the outcome including any rollback
deferred or blocked updates appear on the tech-debt log with a reason and a named remediation path, and are visible to the client in reporting
revisit_triggers: an update breaks a client site in production
a platform or extension announces end of life or is abandoned
the portfolio grows past the point where the window can be completed in one pass

base.update_signal: a production breakage, an out-of-cycle emergency patch, or an end-of-life announcement affecting part of the portfolio

nodes.definition: Keep the portfolio out of the pile that automated attacks harvest, and be honest that this is likelihood reduction rather than immunity. The standing set: unique credentials held in a vault with multi-factor authentication on every panel that offers it; least-privilege accounts on each site with departed staff, former contractors and the leftover administrator from the build removed; unused extensions and themes deleted rather than left installed but inactive, because dormant code is still reachable code; a detection arrangement appropriate to the tier - platform-level scanning, file-change alerts or a security service - with a written triage rule for what it reports; login and file-permission hardening; certificate validity maintained; and periodic review of what each site actually exposes, such as an old upload directory listing or a legacy admin path. The client-facing sentence is written once and used everywhere: this work reduces the chance of compromise and limits what a compromise reaches, and no honest provider promises a site cannot be hacked.

included: credential vaulting and multi-factor coverage
least-privilege user hygiene across sites
removal of unused code
detection arrangement and triage rule
login, permission and exposure hardening
the honest likelihood-reduction statement
excluded: the incident response sequence once something has happened
the client's own device, email and password hygiene beyond advising them
penetration testing or formal security certification

pros.claim: Most small-site compromises come through known, automatable routes that this hygiene closes
pros.example: removing three inactive extensions left over from the build eliminates the exact component that gets exploited a year later

pros.claim: Least-privilege accounts limit what a stolen client login can do
pros.example: a client's assistant phished at their desk cannot install code because their account only edits pages

cons.claim: Hardening adds friction that clients experience as the operator making their own site harder to use
cons.example: an owner who wants one shared password for the whole family business objecting to individual accounts and a second factor

cons.claim: Detection tooling produces noise, and noise trains people to ignore alerts
cons.example: a scanner flagging a benign theme file every week until nobody reads the notifications

failure_modes: leaving the build-era administrator account and its shared password active forever
presenting security work as a guarantee against compromise
buying a security product and treating it as the whole baseline while credentials remain shared and unrotated
hardening the site while the recovery email address for its accounts sits on a long-abandoned mailbox
acceptance_tests: every site's user list has been reviewed within the stated period with unnecessary accounts removed and multi-factor authentication in place wherever the panel supports it
no unused extensions or themes remain installed, and the detection arrangement with its triage rule is recorded per tier
the client-facing wording states likelihood reduction and contains no invulnerability claim
revisit_triggers: a compromise occurs anywhere in the portfolio
a platform or extension class shows a pattern of exploited vulnerabilities
a client's staff changes or an operator contractor's engagement ends

base.update_signal: a compromise, a recurring vulnerability pattern in the stack, or a review finding stale accounts and dormant code

nodes.definition: Instrument the two ways a small site quietly dies: it stops responding, or something expires. Availability is checked from outside the hosting account, because a monitor that lives inside the thing it watches reports nothing when that thing is gone, and the check should request a real page rather than accepting any response. Alongside it run the checks that catch silent failure: certificate validity ahead of expiry, domain expiry watched even when the registrar account belongs to the client, licence and paid-extension renewals, and a periodic proof that the contact or booking form still delivers mail into the client's inbox rather than failing into nothing. All of it lands in one expiry calendar carrying the item, the date, the owning account and the payment instrument, and alerts route to a channel the operator genuinely reads, with thresholds set so that a two-minute blip does not train everyone to ignore the alarm. The purpose is that the operator learns first and calls the client, rather than the client calling to say their website has been down since yesterday.

included: external availability checks against a real page
certificate, domain and licence expiry watching
form-delivery verification
the expiry calendar with owner and payment instrument
alert routing and threshold tuning
excluded: the response once an alert fires, which the incident node owns
marketing analytics and traffic reporting
monitoring the client's third-party vendor platforms the operator does not control

pros.claim: Outside-in checks put the operator ahead of the client on bad news, which is most of what clients mean by feeling looked after
pros.example: messaging a client that their site went down at 6am and is back, before they have opened their laptop

pros.claim: Form-delivery checks catch the most expensive silent failure a small business site has
pros.example: a mail-relay credential change breaking enquiry delivery, caught by a test submission rather than by an empty month

cons.claim: Monitoring generates false alarms and out-of-hours noise that erode the operator's life and attention
cons.example: a supplier's brief nightly maintenance paging the operator every week until thresholds are retuned

failure_modes: monitoring only the home page while the booking system, checkout or form fails unnoticed
watching a domain's expiry only when the operator holds the registrar account, so client-held domains lapse unseen
routing alerts to an address nobody reads at the hours when incidents happen
treating the absence of alerts as proof of health when the monitor itself has silently stopped
acceptance_tests: every enrolled site has an external availability check, a certificate check and a form-delivery verification on a stated interval
the expiry calendar lists domain, certificate and licence dates per site with the owning account and payment instrument, and every entry has a next action date
an alert test has been performed to confirm the routing reaches the operator
revisit_triggers: an outage or expiry was discovered by the client rather than by the monitor
alert volume reaches the level where notifications are being ignored
a site gains a new critical function such as ordering or booking

base.update_signal: an incident or expiry the monitoring set failed to catch, or an alert channel proven unread

nodes.definition: Hold a written sequence for the morning a site is down, defaced, blacklisted, or quietly sending spam, because improvisation under pressure is how small operators make an incident worse and a client former. The sequence: confirm and characterize from outside the account, so the diagnosis is not built on the same broken thing; contain when leaving the site up would harm visitors, by taking it offline or restricting access; notify the client early with the three things they need - what is known, what is being done, and what is not yet known - in plain language and without blame, including when the cause is the supplier's or the operator's own mistake; recover from a restore point verified to predate the compromise rather than the newest copy; close the entry route before returning the site to service, since restoring without closing simply schedules the next incident; and then write a short post-incident note with cause, timeline, client impact and the one procedure change it forces. Where personal data may have been exposed, a notification obligation class may attach with its own deadlines, and the rule is to verify the current requirements in the applicable jurisdiction and advise the client to take their own advice, never to guess or to quietly say nothing.

included: confirm, contain, notify, recover, close, review sequence
restore-point selection that predates a compromise
plain non-blaming client communication including operator-caused incidents
post-incident note and the procedure change it produces
recognizing the breach-notification obligation class
excluded: routine update breakage handled by rollback inside the update cycle
legal advice on notification duties, which the client takes from their own adviser
forensic investigation beyond identifying and closing the entry route

pros.claim: A rehearsed sequence keeps decisions ordered when the operator is stressed and the phone is ringing
pros.example: containing a defaced site and messaging the client within the first fifteen minutes instead of spending an hour trying to fix it silently

pros.claim: Early honest communication retains clients through incidents that would otherwise end the relationship
pros.example: a client who forwards the operator's clear outage note to their own customers, and stays for years afterwards

cons.claim: Contain-first can take a working shopfront offline for hours to protect visitors, which the owner feels immediately
cons.example: a restaurant site pulled during Friday lunch service because it was serving malware to phones

cons.claim: Restoring to a pre-compromise point discards legitimate recent work along with the damage
cons.example: losing two weeks of menu and event updates because the clean generation predates them

failure_modes: restoring a backup that already contains the compromise and calling the incident closed
returning the site to service without closing the entry route, so reinfection follows within days
going quiet with the client while working, so their first real information comes from a customer or a browser warning
blaming the supplier or the client instead of stating facts and the recovery path
acceptance_tests: the playbook exists in writing with the ordered steps, the client notification template and the criteria for taking a site offline
every incident produces a note with cause, timeline, client impact and one procedure change, and the change is reflected in the affected procedure
recovery records show the chosen restore point and the evidence it predates the compromise
revisit_triggers: any incident occurs
a recovery takes materially longer than drills predicted
a notification obligation is triggered or the rules governing one change

base.update_signal: a post-incident review that finds a step missing, mis-ordered, or impossible under real conditions

nodes.definition: Recognize that operating other people's websites means handling other people's personal data - contact and booking form submissions, customer accounts, mailing-list entries, analytics identifiers - and that every backup generation is another copy of it, which attracts an obligation class rather than a preference. The work is practical: map, per site, what personal data it collects and everywhere copies live, including the operator's own inbox when forms are forwarded there and the third-party services the site sends data to; write down the role the operator plays relative to the client for that data and what each side is responsible for; make sure sub-vendors used for hosting, backup storage and mail are engaged on terms that permit the arrangement; set backup retention so a client's deletion request can actually be satisfied within the promised window instead of surviving in copies nobody can reach; and keep a plain-language answer ready for the client's question about what happens if someone asks for their data or if there is a breach. Which regime applies, what a breach-notification deadline is, and whether a written processing agreement is mandatory all vary by jurisdiction and change over time, so the standing rule is to name the obligation class, verify the current rules where the operator and the client each operate, and send the client to their own adviser for advice about their own duties.

included: per-site map of personal data and every copy including backups and forwarding inboxes
the operator's role and responsibility split with the client, in writing
sub-vendor arrangements for hosting, storage and mail
retention set so deletion requests are satisfiable
the verify-current-rules-in-jurisdiction instruction
excluded: legal advice to the client about their own compliance duties
cookie banners and privacy-notice drafting at build time, which delivery handles
the client's marketing consent practices and their own customer database

pros.claim: Knowing where copies live turns a data request from a panic into a procedure
pros.example: answering a deletion request by naming the live database, the backup generations that will age out by a stated date, and the forwarding inbox that was purged

pros.claim: Naming the obligation class instead of guessing specifics keeps the operator honest and out of unlicensed advice
pros.example: telling a client that notification duties may apply and that they should confirm current requirements with their adviser, rather than inventing a deadline

cons.claim: Deletion commitments and long backup retention pull against each other and one of them has to give
cons.example: a promise to erase within a short window that cannot be met while a year of monthly generations is kept for recovery depth

cons.claim: Jurisdictional variation means this node can never supply a final answer, only a disciplined process
cons.example: a client with customers in another region facing rules the operator's own jurisdiction does not impose

failure_modes: forwarding form submissions into a personal inbox that is never included in any data map or retention policy
promising deletion timelines that the backup retention makes impossible
asserting specific legal deadlines or requirements from memory instead of verifying them currently
assuming the client understands that they, not the operator, are usually the party responsible to their own customers
acceptance_tests: each site has a written note of what personal data it collects and every location a copy exists, including backups and forwarded mail
the responsibility split between operator and client is recorded in writing, and sub-vendor arrangements are identified
retention settings are consistent with the deletion window the client was promised, and every regulatory statement carries the instruction to verify current rules in the applicable jurisdiction
revisit_triggers: a site starts collecting a new category of data, such as payments or health-related booking details
a data or deletion request arrives
a sub-vendor, storage location or applicable rule set changes

base.update_signal: a change in applicable rules, a new data category on a site, or a request the current retention design cannot satisfy

nodes.definition: Build the tiers backwards from what the operation demonstrably does. Each tier is a list of promises that already exist as written procedures with known effort: backup frequency and retention, update rhythm and whether staging is used, monitoring coverage, security work, response window, included edit allowance, reporting depth, and any extras such as a periodic performance re-check or a content-update session. The differences between tiers must be things a client can perceive and the operator can evidence - faster response, more frequent copies, staged updates, more included edit time - never adjectives like premium or priority attached to identical work. Anything the operation cannot yet do reliably does not appear in any tier at any price. Two rules protect the model permanently: never promise unlimited quantities of work a human has to perform, because the one client who takes it literally destroys the economics of ten; and never gate a security patch, a breach notification, a backup or an honest incident response behind a higher tier, because those are floor obligations owed to every site under management. Tier design is where the honest version of this business is either encoded or quietly lost.

included: tier contents derived from existing timed procedures
perceivable, evidenceable differences between tiers
the no-unlimited-human-work rule
the floor obligations owed regardless of tier
excluded: setting and positioning the headline price at the offer stage
the sales conversation and objection handling
the site build scope the tier attaches to

pros.claim: Tiers grounded in real procedures can be delivered on the operator's worst week, not just their best
pros.example: a mid tier whose promises survive the month the operator is ill because every item in it is already a batch procedure

pros.claim: Explicit floor obligations prevent the ugliest failure mode in this business, withholding safety from the cheapest clients
pros.example: a critical security patch applied to every site the same day regardless of what each one pays

cons.claim: Honest tiers look thinner on paper than competitors advertising unlimited everything
cons.example: losing a price comparison to a provider promising unlimited edits and guaranteed uptime that they cannot deliver either

cons.claim: More tiers multiply operational variants and the chance of delivering the wrong one
cons.example: four tiers with different backup frequencies producing a site configured for one tier while billed for another

failure_modes: writing tiers from what sounds sellable rather than from what is already procedural
promising unlimited edits, unlimited support or guaranteed uptime
putting security or backup behind the top tier so the lowest-paying sites become the portfolio's infection route
letting tier contents drift per client until no two accounts have the same plan
acceptance_tests: every promise in every tier maps to an existing written procedure with a known effort estimate
no tier contains an unlimited quantity of human work, and the floor obligations are listed as applying to all tiers
each site's configured operations match the tier recorded on its account
revisit_triggers: cost-to-serve measurement shows a tier's contents are not sustainable
cancellation reasons cluster around something a tier promised but did not deliver
an operational capability is added or lost

base.update_signal: measured cost-to-serve, cancellation reasons, or a capability change that contradicts a tier's stated contents

nodes.definition: Define the unit of included work and the exact line at which included work becomes a quoted project, then say it the same way every time. A workable definition names the unit - a request that changes existing content or an existing element and fits within a stated working-time budget - and then lists what is inside it in the client's own vocabulary: text and photo swaps, opening hours, prices and menus, a seasonal banner, publishing a page of supplied content, adding a section that already exists in the design system. It lists what is outside just as concretely: new page templates, redesigns, new functionality, third-party integrations, migrations, content writing, photography and campaign work. It states how unused allowance behaves rather than leaving the client to assume it accumulates, and it states what happens when a request crosses the line - the work is estimated and quoted before anything starts, in the same friendly sentence used with every client. This one page of concrete language is the single largest protector of both the plan's margin and the operator's goodwill, because it converts a monthly negotiation into a shared reference.

included: the request unit and its working-time budget
concrete included and excluded lists in client vocabulary
the rollover rule for unused allowance
the quote trigger and its standard wording
excluded: pre-sale scope negotiation and the build scope agreement
the response-time promise and intake mechanics
the price of quoted project work

pros.claim: Concrete examples end the argument that a policy sentence never settles
pros.example: a client reading 'swapping the photos on your services page is included; designing a new services page is a quote' and simply agreeing

pros.claim: A written boundary lets the operator say yes to small requests generously without fear of it becoming precedent
pros.example: absorbing a two-minute phone-number fix cheerfully because the boundary for real work is already documented elsewhere

cons.claim: Any boundary can be gamed by splitting one project into many small requests
cons.example: a redesign arriving as eleven separate 'small' section changes across three months

cons.claim: Measuring and counting edits costs administrative time and can feel petty to a good client
cons.example: a long-standing client irritated by being told their fourth quick change this month is now billable

failure_modes: defining edits by count alone, so one enormous request consumes the month
leaving rollover unstated until a client claims a year of unused allowance
quoting project work only after starting it, so the client feels ambushed
enforcing the boundary inconsistently across clients, which makes it indefensible with the one who notices
acceptance_tests: the definition names the unit, the working-time budget, at least five concrete included examples and five concrete excluded examples, and the rollover rule
every request that crossed the boundary in the period was quoted and accepted in writing before work started
the same boundary language appears in the tier sheet, the enrollment record and the support reply template
revisit_triggers: requests routinely land in a grey zone the definition does not cover
measured edit minutes exceed the tier's assumption for consecutive periods
a client dispute about what was included

base.update_signal: recurring grey-zone requests or measured edit time drifting past the tier assumption

nodes.definition: Run one intake channel that produces a logged record, a triage class and a response the operator can honor on a bad week rather than an ideal one. Requests arrive by a stated route - an address, a form or a portal - and are logged with client, site, what was asked, and when; a request that arrives by text message at the weekend is answered kindly and then routed into the same log, because unlogged work is invisible to reporting, to the edit allowance and to the cost measurement. Each request is classified: emergency, meaning the site is down, compromised, or its ordering or booking path is broken; time-sensitive, meaning it is tied to a date such as an event, a price change or a holiday closure; or routine. Each class carries a stated first-response window and a stated working-hours boundary, including what actually happens outside those hours, and the promise is calibrated to the week the operator is ill, travelling or already inside another client's incident. A response window that is met ninety-nine times and missed once during a genuine emergency is a strong promise; one that is aspirational on a good day is a monthly apology.

included: the single logged intake channel and the rule for redirecting stray requests into it
triage classes with their first-response windows
the working-hours boundary and what happens outside it
the request log that feeds reporting, allowance counting and cost measurement
excluded: what work is included versus quoted, which the allowance boundary owns
the incident sequence itself once an emergency is confirmed
support for the client's third-party vendors and their platforms

pros.claim: One logged channel makes the work visible, countable and reportable instead of scattered across personal messages
pros.example: a monthly report listing eleven requests with turnaround times because every one was logged, including the two that arrived by text

pros.claim: A conservative promise that is always kept outperforms a fast promise that is sometimes missed
pros.example: a client who tells other business owners the operator always replies the same working day, because they always have

cons.claim: Insisting on one channel fights how small-business owners actually communicate
cons.example: an owner who only ever sends voice messages and finds the request address impersonal

cons.claim: Stated windows become the minimum standard clients hold the operator to even when they were generous
cons.example: a same-day promise cited back during a week when two sites are simultaneously in incident

failure_modes: letting requests arrive anywhere and be answered from memory, so nothing is counted and reporting is guesswork
promising availability that depends on the operator never being ill, travelling or asleep
treating every request as an emergency, which trains clients to escalate everything
answering the loud client first while a quiet one waits, until the quiet one cancels
acceptance_tests: every request in the period appears in the log with its class, receipt time, first response time and completion
the stated response windows were met for the period, and any miss carries a recorded reason
the working-hours boundary and the out-of-hours behaviour are stated in writing to clients
revisit_triggers: response windows are missed more than rarely
request volume grows faster than the book
a tier changes its promised response window

base.update_signal: missed response windows, unlogged work discovered during reporting, or request volume outgrowing capacity

nodes.definition: Measure what one site actually costs to keep every month and compare it to what that client pays, per client rather than on average, because averages hide the two accounts consuming the margin of ten. The measurement adds the direct items the operator can read off their own invoices - the site's share of hosting, backup storage, licences, monitoring, payment processing - to the logged human minutes spent on that site's updates, checks, drills, support, edits and reporting. No market rate is invented anywhere in this node: the inputs are the operator's own records, and any comparison to other providers is a live check made at the time, not a remembered figure. When a site's cost drifts above what its tier assumed, the response follows a ladder in order: fix the cause, which is often one unstable extension or one habit of unlogged phone requests; re-scope the tier, moving the client to a plan that matches how they actually behave; and only then reprice. Repricing is a protocol rather than an event - advance written notice, a plain reason, the same change applied consistently to comparable clients, and an explicit alternative of a lower tier or a clean exit with full handover - because a price rise delivered as a surprise costs more in churn and reputation than the increase collects.

included: per-client direct cost from the operator's own invoices
logged human minutes attributed per site
the fix, re-scope, reprice ladder in order
the repricing protocol with notice, reason, consistency and an exit alternative
excluded: the original offer price and how it was positioned at the sale
any published or assumed market rate for care plans
the client's own pricing and their business economics

pros.claim: Per-client measurement finds the small number of accounts that quietly consume the book's profit
pros.example: discovering that one client's habit of phoning three times a week costs more in minutes than their plan brings in

pros.claim: A protocol makes price changes survivable because the client sees the reasoning and keeps a choice
pros.example: a notice explaining a supplier increase, offering a lower tier, and keeping almost every account through the change

cons.claim: Time logging is administrative overhead that solo operators abandon first when busy
cons.example: three months of untracked minutes making the next repricing decision a guess again

cons.claim: Repricing always loses some accounts, including ones whose loss was not worth the increase
cons.example: a long-standing client leaving over a modest rise that would have taken a year to pay back the acquisition cost of replacing them

failure_modes: pricing changes made on a feeling of being underpaid rather than on measured cost
raising prices silently in the invoice and hoping nobody reads it
applying an increase to the clients who complain least while the demanding accounts stay cheap
quoting or benchmarking against remembered figures for what others charge instead of checking currently
acceptance_tests: each active account has a current cost-to-serve figure built from the operator's own invoices and logged minutes, with the measurement period stated
every price change was preceded by written notice with a plain reason, was applied consistently across comparable accounts, and offered a lower tier or a clean exit
no statement of a market rate appears anywhere in the pricing rationale unless it is a dated live quote from a named source
revisit_triggers: supplier or licence costs change
a client's support pattern changes materially
measured cost exceeds the tier assumption for consecutive periods
churn follows a price change more heavily than expected

base.update_signal: a supplier price change, a shift in a client's support pattern, or a repricing round whose churn differs from expectation

nodes.definition: Solve the structural problem of maintenance work: when it succeeds, nothing happens, and the client receives an invoice for silence. The monthly report is short, factual and specific to that site - updates applied and any deferred with the reason, backups taken and the date of the last verified restore point, availability as observed by the named monitor over the period, security events and what was done about them, requests received and completed with their turnaround, expiries coming up and who needs to act, and one recommendation worth reading. Beyond the artifact, the cadence includes a human conversation on a slower rhythm: a call each quarter where that suits the client, and at minimum a yearly review covering whether the content still matches the business, what has aged in the platform, what the site is not doing that the owner now needs, and what any of it would cost. Renewals are won in that conversation far more than in the monthly attachment, and it is where a rebuild gets proposed while there is still time to plan one. Every line of it must be traceable to a record the client could ask to see.

included: the monthly report contents traceable to operational records
the deferred-work and upcoming-expiry disclosures
the quarterly or yearly review conversation and its agenda
one actionable recommendation per report
excluded: marketing performance claims and outcome promises, which claim integrity governs
running the client's analytics or advertising
the sales pitch for a new build, beyond naming when a rebuild becomes the honest recommendation

pros.claim: A specific report converts silence into visible value and is the cheapest retention instrument available
pros.example: a client forwarding the report to a partner as the reason they keep paying the monthly fee

pros.claim: The yearly review surfaces work the client wants before they go looking elsewhere for it
pros.example: an owner mentioning a new service line in the review call, which becomes a quoted project instead of a competitor's opportunity

cons.claim: Reports cost real time every month across the whole book and many clients never open them
cons.example: an hour a month producing reports for a client who has not clicked one in a year

cons.claim: Detailed reporting invites scrutiny of quiet months where genuinely little needed doing
cons.example: a client asking why they pay the same for a month whose report shows two updates and no incidents

failure_modes: padding reports with vanity numbers to look busy
reporting work that was not actually performed because the log was reconstructed from memory
sending reports while never having a conversation, so the relationship is entirely mechanical when a renewal decision arrives
hiding deferred updates and known tech debt so the client is surprised by a rebuild recommendation
acceptance_tests: each report's items reconcile to the update log, backup and drill records, monitor data and request log for that period
deferred work and upcoming expiries appear in the report rather than only in internal notes
each account has a recorded review conversation within the stated period
revisit_triggers: a client says the report does not tell them anything useful
reports are consistently unopened across the book
a cancellation cites not knowing what the plan did

base.update_signal: client feedback that the report is not useful, or a cancellation citing invisible value

nodes.definition: Govern what may be said to a client about results, because in this industry the easiest sale and the fastest reputational death share the same sentence. The rules: never guarantee rankings, traffic, enquiries or revenue, in any tier, proposal, report or renewal conversation, and never imply it with softer words either; report availability as observed by a named monitor over a stated period rather than as a guaranteed percentage the operator does not control upstream, and pass through no supplier commitment as if it were the operator's own; state performance and accessibility as a measurement of a named page with the tool and date attached, never as a permanent property of the site; present analytics with what they can and cannot show, since a small business's month-to-month movement is mostly noise and a rise after a change is not proof the change caused it; and say nothing the operator could not immediately show the client the evidence for. When a client asks for a guarantee, the honest reply names what genuinely is guaranteed - the work performed on schedule, the response window, the recoverability that drills have demonstrated - and states plainly what is not. This node is a constraint on other people's enthusiasm, including the operator's own during a renewal conversation.

included: the prohibition on ranking, traffic, lead and revenue guarantees
observed-versus-guaranteed availability language
per-page, per-date, per-tool performance and accessibility statements
honest analytics framing including noise and causation limits
the evidence-on-request standard
excluded: the technical measurement work at build time, which delivery performs
the client's own advertising claims about their business
search or content strategy services, which are outside this business entirely

pros.claim: Refusing outcome guarantees eliminates the disputes that end relationships and reputations
pros.example: a client who cannot claim a refund for lost rankings because nothing about rankings was ever promised

pros.claim: Evidence-backed statements build the kind of trust that survives an incident
pros.example: a client believing the recovery estimate because every previous number they were given proved checkable

cons.claim: Honest limits lose deals and renewals to competitors willing to promise outcomes
cons.example: a client moving to a provider guaranteeing first-page results, and sometimes not returning

cons.claim: Careful qualification can read as evasive to an owner who just wants a straight answer
cons.example: an owner hearing 'we cannot promise more enquiries' as the operator not believing in their own work

failure_modes: repeating a supplier's uptime figure to clients as the operator's guarantee
quoting a one-off performance score as a permanent property of the site
attributing a traffic rise to the care plan in a report
letting a renewal conversation drift into implied promises that the written materials never make
acceptance_tests: no client-facing artifact contains a ranking, traffic, lead or revenue guarantee, and availability appears only as observed by a named monitor over a stated period
every performance or accessibility statement names the page, the tool and the date of measurement
for any number in a report, the underlying record can be produced on request
revisit_triggers: a client reports having understood a promise the operator did not intend to make
a competitor claim pressures the operator to match outcome language
a new metric or tool enters the reporting set

base.update_signal: a client misunderstanding traced to the operator's wording, or a new claim type entering client-facing material

nodes.definition: Watch for the indicators that an account is drifting and act while there is still something to repair. The reliable ones in this business: edit requests stop entirely for months on an account that used to send them; the report is never opened or acknowledged; a card fails; the champion contact leaves or the business changes hands; the owner asks what exactly they are paying for each month; a renewal question arrives with a competitor's proposal attached; the client's own business is visibly struggling. Each signal gets a diagnosis before a response, because the four underlying causes need opposite treatments: the plan is wrong for how they actually behave, a promise is being missed, the value is real but invisible, or the business itself is ending. The legitimate responses are to fix the failing promise, right-size the tier, make the work visible with a specific conversation, or help them leave well. A discount offered to a client whose real complaint is a missed response window buys one month and confirms to them that they were overpaying all along.

included: the leading-indicator list specific to small-site care accounts
the four-cause diagnosis before any response
the legitimate response set including helping a client leave
the rule against reflex discounting
excluded: the ethical limits on persuasion themselves, which the guardrails node defines
payment retry and suspension mechanics
winning back clients who have already gone

pros.claim: Leading signals give weeks of warning, which is the difference between a save and a notification
pros.example: noticing four months of silence and a bounced report, and opening a conversation before the cancellation email arrives

pros.claim: Diagnosing first stops the operator from paying to keep a client who was never unhappy about price
pros.example: a client who cancelled a discount offer but stayed after one missed request was acknowledged and fixed

cons.claim: Signals produce false positives, and treating a quiet, contented client as a flight risk can create the doubt it was trying to prevent
cons.example: a check-in that asks whether the plan is still worth it and plants the question in an owner who had not considered it

cons.claim: Triage takes attention away from delivery, and the book that is not maintained generates the next wave of signals
cons.example: a month spent on retention calls while the update round slips and two sites break

failure_modes: reading every signal as a price objection and discounting reflexively
waiting for the cancellation email as the first signal
chasing an account whose business is genuinely closing instead of offering a graceful exit
diagnosing from assumption rather than asking the client a direct question
acceptance_tests: each account carries a current signal status reviewed on a stated cadence, with the signals that fired recorded
every retention response in the period is preceded by a recorded diagnosis naming which of the four causes it addresses
no discount was issued without a recorded diagnosis showing price was the actual cause
revisit_triggers: a cancellation arrives with no signal having fired
cancellation reasons cluster around one promise or one tier
a save tactic is repeatedly failing

base.update_signal: cancellations that fired no signal, or a pattern in stated cancellation reasons

nodes.definition: Handle money not arriving without letting a card expiry become a lost client or an ugly standoff.
