The elements are ordered and dull on purpose: charge on the stated date and send a receipt; detect the failure automatically rather than at month end; retry on a schedule that respects the payment network's own rules; then contact a human through a channel a human reads, with a plainly worded message that says what failed and exactly how to fix it, written as a reminder rather than a warning because most failures are an expired card, a changed bank or a billing email nobody monitors, not a refusal to pay. Escalation follows a ladder with stated dates that the client agreed at enrollment, ending in service suspension only after written notice and only per those terms. Throughout, the client's domain, content, database and backups remain available and untouched: an unpaid invoice is a debt to be collected through the terms and, if necessary, ordinary collections, never a reason to hold a small business's website hostage, and any suspension is of the operator's own labour and hosting custody, disclosed in advance, with the assets released on request regardless.

included: automatic failure detection and scheduled retries
the plainly worded human message and the channel it uses
the pre-agreed escalation ladder with dates ending in suspension after written notice
the absolute separation of debt collection from client-owned assets
excluded: deciding the price or the tier
voluntary cancellation handling and exit conversations
legal debt-recovery advice, which the operator takes from their own adviser

pros.claim: Most failed payments are mechanical and recover on a friendly reminder, making this the cheapest churn to prevent
pros.example: an expired card replaced within an hour of a message that read like a reminder rather than a demand

pros.claim: Pre-agreed terms let the operator act on a genuine non-payer without improvising a policy under pressure
pros.example: a suspension that follows dates the client accepted at enrollment, with the exit pack offered in the same message

cons.claim: Refusing to use asset control as leverage means some debts are simply never collected
cons.example: a closing business that stops paying, keeps its domain and content, and leaves the last invoices unpaid

cons.claim: Long grace periods fund service for accounts that will never pay again
cons.example: three months of updates, backups and monitoring delivered to a client who had already decided to close

failure_modes: suspending or deleting a site without the notice the client agreed to
withholding a domain, database, backup or credentials to force payment
letting the first notice read as an accusation, which turns a card expiry into a cancellation
chasing by an automated email loop only, so a genuine problem never reaches a human
acceptance_tests: the escalation ladder with its dates and the suspension conditions is recorded in terms the client accepted at enrollment
every dunning sequence in the period shows automated detection, a retry attempt, and a human-readable message before any escalation
no case exists in which client-owned assets were withheld, and any suspension was preceded by written notice
revisit_triggers: payment failure rates rise or a payment provider changes its retry rules
a suspension leads to a dispute or a complaint
recovery messaging is producing cancellations rather than card updates

base.update_signal: a change in payment failure rates, provider retry rules, or a dispute arising from an escalation

nodes.definition: Fix the limits on how a recurring account may be retained, and treat them as outranking the retention target. No fear-selling: the risk of running an unmaintained site is explained once, factually, including what maintenance does and does not prevent, and never dressed up as a prediction that their site will be hacked or destroyed if they cancel. No manufactured urgency, no invented consequences of leaving, and no implying that the site will stop working simply because the plan ends when it will not. Disclosure first: price changes, supplier migrations, tier changes and anything that will be billed are disclosed in writing before they happen, not discovered in an invoice. Cancellation is as easy as signing up, handled through the same channel, without a retention gauntlet, a hidden notice period or a form designed to be missed. And extra care wherever the client cannot evaluate the technical claims - an older owner, a first-time business, someone who inherited the site from a relative or a departed employee - which means plain language, offering the cheaper option when it genuinely fits, confirming the client understood rather than exploiting that they did not, and being willing to tell a client that they do not need the plan they are asking to buy. An account kept by frightening someone who could not assess the claim is a liability wearing the costume of revenue.

included: the no-fear-selling and no-manufactured-urgency rules
disclosure before any price, supplier or billing change
cancellation as easy as signup
heightened care for clients who cannot evaluate technical claims
the duty to talk a client out of a plan they do not need
excluded: the acquisition-stage selling ethics that govern the original offer conversation
the mechanics of detecting churn signals
consumer-law specifics, which are named as an obligation class and verified locally

pros.claim: Guardrails protect the referral engine that a small local reseller lives on
pros.example: an owner who left cleanly and still recommends the operator to two other businesses in the same street

pros.claim: Refusing to oversell keeps the book made of accounts that renew willingly rather than accounts that resent the invoice
pros.example: steering a seasonal client onto the smallest plan and keeping them for years instead of losing them in month four

cons.claim: Honest framing loses accounts that fear-based pitches would have kept, and the loss is immediate while the reputational gain is slow
cons.example: a client cancelling after being told plainly that their static site is at low risk and the middle tier is more than they need

cons.claim: Frictionless cancellation removes the pause in which a genuine misunderstanding could have been corrected
cons.example: an account closing over a billing confusion that one conversation would have resolved

failure_modes: describing worst-case security outcomes as likely to a client who cannot judge the claim
burying a notice period or an auto-renewal term the client never saw
letting a save attempt become pressure on someone who has already said no
selling a higher tier to the least technical client precisely because they will not question it
acceptance_tests: client-facing retention and renewal material contains no prediction of harm used as a lever and no urgency the facts do not support
cancellation can be completed through the same channel as signup, and the notice terms match what the client agreed at enrollment
for clients flagged as unable to evaluate technical claims, the record shows plain-language explanation and confirmed understanding, including any case where a cheaper option was recommended
revisit_triggers: a client says they felt pressured or misled
a save tactic in use starts relying on fear or urgency
consumer-protection or cancellation rules in the operating jurisdiction change

base.update_signal: a complaint about pressure or misunderstanding, or a change in consumer-protection rules where the operator sells

nodes.definition: Former clients are the warmest list a small reseller has, and reactivation is mostly an honest technical assessment attached to a graceful message. The work: keep a record of who left, when, why in their own words, and what state their site was in at handover; before any approach, look at what actually happened since - is the site still up, is the platform years behind, has it been defaced or filled with spam pages, did the domain lapse or the certificate expire, did the forms stop delivering; and lead with the specific, checkable finding rather than a generic note about missing them. The rules that keep this from becoming the industry's worst behaviour: no campaign built on frightening someone with what was found, only a factual description and an offer; state plainly that an aged site usually needs remediation priced as a project before it can enter a care plan again, rather than implying the monthly fee alone will fix it; and take a no the first time it is given. A client who left because of a genuine service failure is approached only after that failure has actually been fixed, and the approach acknowledges it.

included: the departure record with reason and state at handover
a current technical assessment before any approach
factual, non-frightening outreach and the remediation-as-project rule
the accept-a-no-the-first-time rule and the fixed-failure precondition
excluded: acquisition of clients who were never customers
offboarding itself
free remedial work performed as an inducement to return

pros.claim: A specific finding earns a reply where a generic reconnection message does not
pros.example: a short note that their certificate expired last week and visitors are seeing a browser warning, with no pitch attached

pros.claim: Former clients already know how the operator works, so re-entry skips most of the trust-building cost
pros.example: a client returning after a cheaper provider stopped answering, needing only a remediation quote and a start date

cons.claim: Aged sites often need more remediation than the returning client expects to pay for, which can sour the reunion
cons.example: a two-year-old platform requiring a rebuild rather than the plan renewal the owner had in mind

cons.claim: Outreach based on findings sits close to a line that is easy to cross into alarmism
cons.example: a message describing security exposure in a tone that reads as a scare tactic rather than a courtesy

failure_modes: building a campaign around alarming findings
pitching a care plan onto a site whose real need is a rebuild, so the plan starts already failing
repeated approaches after a clear no
approaching a client who left over an unfixed service failure as though nothing happened
acceptance_tests: every reactivation approach records the current site findings it is based on and the date they were checked
any approach involving remediation states that the remediation is a separately quoted project before plan re-entry
no client appears in a second approach after declining once, and any client who left over a service failure was approached only after the fix was recorded
revisit_triggers: reactivation attempts consistently produce no replies or negative responses
returning clients repeatedly arrive in worse technical condition than the assessment predicted
a former client asks not to be contacted

base.update_signal: reactivation response patterns, or returning sites whose condition differs systematically from the pre-approach assessment

nodes.definition: Run the portfolio as a book rather than as a pile of individual favours. Capacity is bounded by the recurring hours the book already consumes - update rounds, checks, drills, reports, support minutes - plus the reserve required for incidents and for the build work that funds the business; when new enrollments eat that reserve, promises start slipping before the operator consciously notices, so the honest response is to pause enrollment, standardize, or trim the book first rather than to absorb it and hope. On a stated cadence, every account is reviewed against four readings: margin against its measured cost-to-serve, support load, payment reliability, and relationship quality including whether the client treats the operator decently. Each review produces exactly one decision per account - keep as is, right-size the tier, reprice with notice, standardize the outlier by migrating a snowflake site onto the portfolio stack, or offboard gracefully - and the decision is recorded with its reason so the next review can see whether it worked. Releasing a client is a legitimate, respectful, well-executed operation with a full handover, not an admission of failure.

included: capacity expressed as recurring hours plus incident and build reserve
the enrollment pause rule when reserve is consumed
the four review readings per account
one recorded decision per account per review including graceful release
excluded: acquiring new clients and the sales pipeline
the price-change protocol mechanics themselves
the delivery capacity of the build pipeline

pros.claim: A capacity limit protects the promises already sold from being diluted by the next sale
pros.example: pausing enrollment for a month so the update round and two overdue drills are actually completed

pros.claim: Reviewing account by account exposes the handful of accounts that make the whole book feel unmanageable
pros.example: two clients accounting for most of the month's support minutes, one right-sized and one released

cons.claim: Turning away or releasing revenue is painful and easy to postpone, especially in a slow month for builds
cons.example: accepting three more sites during a quiet quarter and missing the next two update windows across the portfolio

cons.claim: Judging relationship quality is subjective and can rationalize releasing a client who was merely demanding but fair
cons.example: labelling a detail-oriented client as difficult when the real problem was an unclear edit boundary

failure_modes: measuring capacity only in money rather than in the hours the book actually consumes
enrolling past the reserve and discovering it through missed windows and unhappy clients
reviewing the book without producing a decision, so the same problem accounts persist for years
releasing a client abruptly rather than through the full offboarding process
acceptance_tests: the current recurring hour load and the reserve are written down, with the enrollment ceiling that follows from them
each account has a dated review record with the four readings and exactly one decision with its reason
every release decision is executed through the standard offboarding handover rather than an abrupt termination
revisit_triggers: windows, drills or reports start slipping
the operator's available hours change through illness, hiring or other work
a small number of accounts begin dominating support load

base.update_signal: slipped operational windows, a change in available hours, or review decisions that failed to hold at the next review

nodes.definition: Make leaving clean, complete and fast, because the exit is where the ownership promise is either proven or exposed as marketing. The handover pack contains a full export of the site files and database, the media library, a current backup the client can hold themselves, the DNS zone as it stands, the account inventory naming the owner and the takeover route for each, the runbook, and any assets produced during the relationship - delivered to the client or their new provider on a stated timeline, followed by removal of the operator's delegated access and a confirmation that it is gone. The process also includes a short exit conversation that records the real reason for leaving in the client's own words, a final invoice with no surprise charges, an explicit statement of the date on which service, monitoring and backups end so the client is never silently unprotected while believing otherwise, guidance on what their new provider will need, and an open door. Nothing in the pack is withheld pending payment of anything, and nothing about the process is designed to make leaving slow.

included: the complete handover pack contents and delivery timeline
access wind-down with confirmation
the exit conversation capturing the real reason
the explicit end-of-protection date and final invoice
the no-withholding rule
excluded: the commercial decision to end the relationship, on either side
performing migration work for the new provider beyond supplying assets and answering reasonable questions
ongoing support after the stated end date

pros.claim: A clean exit converts a lost client into a neutral or positive reference in a small local market where word travels
pros.example: a departing owner telling their business network that getting everything back took one email and two days

pros.claim: A rehearsed exit pack means the operator can promise portability truthfully at every sale afterwards
pros.example: answering a prospect's lock-in question by describing exactly what a leaving client receives and how quickly

cons.claim: Producing a genuine handover pack costs unbillable hours at precisely the moment the revenue stops
cons.example: half a day exporting, packaging and documenting for an account that has already sent its last payment

cons.claim: Complete portability removes every commercial obstacle to leaving, including the ones a weaker operator would rely on
cons.example: a client moving to a cheaper provider in a week because nothing technical stood in their way

failure_modes: delaying or partially delivering the pack while an invoice is disputed
leaving operator access in place afterwards, which is both a security exposure and a false impression of continued protection
failing to state when monitoring and backups stop, so the client believes they are covered when they are not
skipping the exit conversation and therefore never learning the actual reason for the loss
acceptance_tests: the pack delivered contains files, database, media, a holdable backup, the DNS zone, the account inventory with takeover routes, and the runbook, with the delivery date recorded
operator access removal is confirmed and dated, and the client has written confirmation of when service, monitoring and backups end
no element of the handover was made conditional on payment, and the recorded exit reason exists in the client's own words
revisit_triggers: a departing client or their new provider reports something missing from the pack
an exit takes longer than the stated timeline
the stack or hosting arrangement changes what a complete export contains

base.update_signal: a handover where something was missing, delayed, or made conditional, or a stack change altering what a complete export includes

edges.why_related: the promise set decides how much containment, portability and hands-off automation the hosting layout has to provide
the client-ownership principle in the charter is only real once it exists as a per-account ledger with a revocable access model
supplier concentration and the migration rehearsal can only be assessed once the tenancy model and platform features in use are fixed
what intake must verify on each site is determined by where sites live and which capabilities the platform provides versus which are run by hand
intake cannot confirm access, recovery addresses and expiries without the register structure to record them into
the regime is applied and verified per site at intake, and intake supplies the change-rate and business-criticality facts the regime is derived from
there is nothing to rehearse until scope, frequency, location and retention are defined
a proven rollback path is the precondition that makes routine updating an acceptable risk rather than a gamble
patching is the load-bearing part of the hygiene set, and the baseline's other work assumes updates are already happening on a rhythm
monitors, alert routing and every expiry date enter the calendar at enrollment, and unenrolled sites are unwatched sites
the playbook starts from a detection event, so its speed is bounded by what monitoring actually notices and where the alert lands
a tier may only promise the update rhythm, staging behaviour and check depth the cycle can actually perform across the whole book
the allowance is a tier component, so its unit, size and rollover rule are defined inside the tier structure
response windows are tier promises, so triage classes and windows are set where the tiers are defined
the request log is the only honest source of the human minutes that dominate per-client cost
the report exists to evidence exactly the promises the tier makes, so its sections are derived from the tier contents
the exit pack is the register plus exports, so a stale register makes a complete handover impossible
every figure and phrase in the report and the review conversation must pass the verifiability and no-guarantee rules before it is sent
edges.benefit_of_coupling: the report becomes evidence rather than persuasion, which is what makes it defensible under scrutiny
edges.risk_of_conflict: the constraint strips out the outcome numbers a client would find most emotionally satisfying

edges.why_related: collection messaging, escalation dates and suspension are bounded by the disclosure-first and no-leverage rules
edges.benefit_of_coupling: recovery stays a reminder process rather than a pressure campaign, which recovers more cards and fewer complaints
edges.risk_of_conflict: some genuinely owed money becomes uncollectable without leverage

edges.why_related: outreach built on technical findings is exactly where alarmism is tempting, so the no-fear-selling rule governs every reactivation message
edges.benefit_of_coupling: the operator can send findings-based outreach at all without becoming the industry's scare-mail problem
edges.risk_of_conflict: the factual version of a finding converts fewer former clients than an alarming one would

edges.why_related: retention depth is capped by what the deletion commitments and the data map allow, since every generation is another copy of personal data
edges.benefit_of_coupling: deletion requests remain satisfiable instead of surviving invisibly in old copies
edges.risk_of_conflict: shorter retention shrinks the window in which a late-detected compromise still has a clean generation to restore from

edges.why_related: no tier may promise availability, recovery speed or features beyond what the supplier commitment and the operator's own procedures can support
edges.benefit_of_coupling: tier promises stay inside what can actually be delivered when the supplier is the limiting factor
edges.risk_of_conflict: the honest ceiling looks weaker than competitors passing supplier marketing through as guarantees

edges.why_related: enrollment is gated by remaining capacity, because a site accepted past the reserve degrades promises already sold to everyone else
edges.benefit_of_coupling: existing clients keep the service they pay for instead of subsidizing growth with slipped windows
edges.risk_of_conflict: revenue is refused or delayed in exactly the months when it feels hardest to refuse

edges.why_related: storage, off-account copies and drill hours are a visible cost that the cheapest tier's economics constantly argue against
edges.resolution_rule: the minimum viable recoverability - a verified off-account copy and a demonstrated restore - is a floor obligation on every site regardless of tier; if a tier's economics cannot fund the floor, the tier's contents or its price change, never the backup floor

edges.why_related: interrupting a batch window to answer requests inside the promised response time is what makes both the window and the promise slip
edges.resolution_rule: emergencies interrupt the window immediately; time-sensitive and routine requests get an acknowledgement inside the promised window and are scheduled after it, and if that pattern breaks the promise repeatedly the window is split into smaller batches rather than the promise being quietly abandoned

edges.why_related: the moment an account looks like leaving is exactly when absorbing out-of-scope work feels cheaper than defending the boundary
edges.resolution_rule: one documented goodwill exception may be granted and named as an exception to the client; anything further is quoted as a project, and if boundary friction is the actual churn cause the fix is to change the tier or the boundary definition in writing for everyone, not to run a silent unlimited plan for one account

edges.why_related: the most effective short-term save tactics - implied risk, urgency, friction on the way out - are the ones the guardrails forbid
edges.resolution_rule: the guardrails dominate without exception; a save may only offer facts, a fix, a right-sized tier or a graceful exit, and any tactic that would not survive being read aloud to the client's family is not used even when the account is lost by refusing it

edges.why_related: an unpaid balance creates the standing temptation to slow or condition the handover of assets the client owns
edges.resolution_rule: asset ownership dominates absolutely - the handover pack is delivered on the normal timeline regardless of any balance owed, while the debt is pursued through the agreed terms and ordinary collections; the only permitted withholding is the operator's own future labour and hosting custody, after written notice on the pre-agreed dates

edges.why_related: the densest, cheapest, most automated supplier arrangement is usually the one whose proprietary features are hardest to leave
edges.resolution_rule: portability wins when a feature would make a single site unexportable or a migration untestable; supplier convenience wins where a tested export path still exists, and any newly adopted proprietary dependency is recorded with its replacement cost at the moment it is adopted

edges.why_related: updates are themselves a leading cause of client-visible breakage, so update activity produces a predictable share of incidents
edges.example: a platform update that silently disables a form plugin, discovered as an incident when enquiries stop arriving

edges.why_related: reporting quality and conversation frequency drive whether the value of invisible work is perceived, which is what most cancellation signals are actually measuring
edges.example: an account that stops opening reports and cancels four months later citing not knowing what the fee covered

edges.why_related: the tenancy and isolation model determines how far a single compromise can travel and therefore how much the hygiene set has to carry
edges.example: shared account layouts turning one vulnerable extension into a portfolio-wide cleanup

edges.why_related: when triage concludes that leaving is the right outcome for the client, the process moves directly into the standard handover rather than into persuasion
the exit record - reason in the client's words, state at handover, date - is the input any later reactivation assessment starts from
each post-incident note names one procedure change, and update policy is the procedure it most often changes
edges.benefit_of_coupling: the same failure does not recur across the rest of the portfolio

edges.why_related: measured per-client cost is the evidence that a tier's contents are unsustainable and must be re-scoped rather than merely repriced
edges.benefit_of_coupling: tiers converge on what the operation can actually deliver profitably instead of drifting further from it

edges.why_related: capacity truth is what proves a charter promise unrealistic, forcing the promise set to be revised rather than quietly missed
edges.benefit_of_coupling: the charter stays a description of what happens rather than an aspiration nobody meets

edges.why_related: both rest on the same capability - producing a complete, portable copy of a site that works somewhere other than where it lives now
edges.benefit_of_coupling: investing in a clean export path pays twice, once as recoverability and once as a credible exit promise

conflict_axes.name: density_margin_vs_blast_radius
conflict_axes.description: Packing many client sites into one cheap, shared supplier arrangement lowers cost per site and simplifies administration, while isolating each site limits what a single compromise, suspension or resource spike can reach.
poles: maximize density and margin per site
maximize isolation between clients
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: accept density only where a per-site isolation boundary and a tested per-site export both exist; where either is missing, pay for separation

conflict_axes.name: patch_speed_vs_update_stability
conflict_axes.description: Applying fixes the day they appear closes exposure windows but raises the chance of breaking a working site; batching and staging protects stability but leaves known vulnerabilities open longer.
poles: patch immediately on disclosure
batch, stage and verify before applying
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: split the stream - actively exploited security fixes take the fast path with a restore point, everything else waits for the batched window with its functional walk

conflict_axes.name: tier_generosity_vs_sustainable_cost
conflict_axes.description: Generous inclusions and unlimited-sounding promises win comparisons and feel good to deliver, while measured cost-to-serve says which of them quietly destroy the plan's economics.
poles: promise more to win and keep accounts
promise only what measurement shows is sustainable
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: make inclusions concrete and bounded, and convert generosity into named, occasional goodwill exceptions rather than standing promises

conflict_axes.name: proof_of_value_vs_claim_honesty
conflict_axes.description: Clients judge a care plan by outcomes they can feel - enquiries, sales, rankings - while the operator can only honestly evidence work performed, availability observed and recoverability demonstrated.
poles: show the outcome numbers the client wants
report only what can be evidenced and never guarantee outcomes
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: lead the report with specific work and measured availability, present analytics with their limits stated, and answer guarantee requests by naming precisely what is and is not guaranteed

conflict_axes.name: retention_pressure_vs_ethical_persuasion
conflict_axes.description: The tactics that save accounts fastest - implied risk, urgency, exit friction, selling up to the least technical client - are precisely the ones that damage a local reputation and exploit the people least able to judge.
poles: save the account by any legal means
persuade only with facts the client can verify
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: restrict saves to fixing a failing promise, right-sizing the tier, making value visible, or helping the client leave well, with heightened care wherever the client cannot assess the claim

conflict_axes.name: standardization_vs_client_specific_accommodation
conflict_axes.description: A uniform stack, schedule and procedure is what makes a one-person portfolio operable at all, while individual clients keep asking for arrangements that only make sense for them.
poles: keep every site on the same procedures
accommodate each client's preference
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: accommodate in content and communication, refuse in infrastructure and schedule, and migrate existing snowflakes onto the standard at the next natural opportunity

conflict_axes.name: supplier_convenience_vs_portability
conflict_axes.description: The supplier's deepest automation removes hours of manual work and the same automation is often what makes a site impossible to move without loss.
poles: adopt supplier features that save operator time
keep every site exportable and restorable elsewhere
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: adopt convenience only above a tested export path, and record the replacement cost of each proprietary dependency at the moment it is adopted

conflict_axes.name: availability_promise_vs_solo_capacity
conflict_axes.description: Clients want to feel covered at all hours, and one operator cannot be awake, well and unoccupied at all hours without either breaking the promise or breaking themselves.
poles: promise fast response whenever trouble strikes
promise only what a single person can keep on a bad week
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: state working hours and out-of-hours behaviour explicitly, reserve emergency interruption for genuine emergencies, and buy or partner for cover before promising beyond one person

conflict_axes.name: deletion_duty_vs_recovery_depth
conflict_axes.description: Long backup retention is what rescues a site from a compromise nobody noticed for weeks, and every retained generation is another copy of personal data the operator has undertaken to be able to delete.
poles: keep generations long enough to outlast detection lag
keep only what deletion commitments allow
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: set retention from detection-lag reasoning first, then reconcile it with the deletion window actually promised, and disclose the resulting behaviour to the client rather than promising both extremes

conflict_axes.name: collections_leverage_vs_client_asset_ownership
conflict_axes.description: The operator holds the practical means to make leaving or not paying painful, and the entire positioning of the business rests on never using it.
poles: use access and custody as leverage for payment
release client-owned assets unconditionally
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: separate the two ledgers permanently - assets are released on request regardless of balance, while unpaid work is pursued through the agreed terms and, if necessary, ordinary collections

edge_cases.description: A widely exploited vulnerability in a common extension is disclosed the day after the batch window closed, and several portfolio sites run it
edge_cases.trigger: an actively exploited flaw lands between scheduled update windows
edge_cases.mitigation: run the security fast path immediately across affected sites with a restore point each, notify clients of the out-of-cycle change, and record the deviation in the next report rather than hiding it

edge_cases.description: The upstream supplier has a multi-hour outage; every site is down, nothing the operator does changes it, and clients are calling
edge_cases.trigger: a supplier-side failure the operator cannot fix
edge_cases.mitigation: send one factual update naming the supplier issue, what is known and the next update time, without passing through supplier promises as the operator's own; log the outage against the switch triggers and decide afterwards, not during

edge_cases.description: A restore is needed, but the compromise turns out to predate every retained generation, so the newest clean copy is older than the retention window
edge_cases.mitigation: rebuild the site's code layer from the original build sources while preserving content from the infected copy after inspection, tell the client plainly what is lost, and extend retention or add detection so the same gap cannot recur

edge_cases.description: A client asks for all their customer data to be deleted while backup generations still contain copies of it
edge_cases.trigger: a deletion request arrives against data that lives in retained backups
edge_cases.mitigation: delete from the live systems immediately, state in writing which backup generations still hold copies and the date they age out, keep those generations access-restricted meanwhile, and verify the current requirement in the applicable jurisdiction rather than improvising a rule

edge_cases.description: A client's card has failed for weeks, they are not replying, and the suspension date named in their terms is approaching
edge_cases.trigger: silence during the dunning ladder as the suspension date arrives
edge_cases.mitigation: make one final contact attempt through a different channel including a phone call, suspend only the operator's own labour and custody exactly as the agreed terms allow, keep the domain, content and backups intact and available, and send the handover pack offer with the suspension notice

edge_cases.description: A client insists the care plan should be improving their search rankings and threatens to leave because traffic is flat
edge_cases.trigger: an outcome expectation the plan never promised surfaces at renewal
edge_cases.mitigation: restate what the plan does and does not cover from the written tier, show the evidence of work performed, explain plainly why no honest provider guarantees rankings, and either quote the separate work they actually want or help them leave without a fight

edge_cases.description: The business is sold and the new owner has never heard of the care plan, has no idea what the monthly charge is, and controls none of the accounts
edge_cases.trigger: a change of business ownership mid-plan
edge_cases.mitigation: treat it as a re-enrollment - re-explain the plan in plain language to the new owner, re-verify ownership and recovery addresses in the register, confirm billing afresh, and accept a clean exit with full handover if they do not want the service

edge_cases.description: A site cannot be updated because a custom feature built years ago breaks with the current platform version, and the version is nearing end of life
edge_cases.trigger: a customization blocks updating on a platform approaching end of life
edge_cases.mitigation: log the tech debt with its end-of-life date, disclose the blocked updates in the report rather than reporting the site as maintained, present the rebuild-or-replace options with their costs early, and record the client's decision if they choose to run on knowingly

edge_cases.description: A client sends a stream of individually tiny requests that each fit the allowance but together amount to a redesign
edge_cases.trigger: project-sized work arriving as many small requests
edge_cases.mitigation: name the pattern early and kindly using the logged requests as evidence, propose the project scope and quote it, and if the client prefers to continue piecemeal, move them to the tier whose measured allowance matches their behaviour

edge_cases.description: The client's own third-party vendor breaks - a booking widget, payment gateway or review feed - and the client calls the operator at nine in the evening
edge_cases.trigger: a failure inside a vendor the client contracts directly
edge_cases.mitigation: confirm quickly whether the site itself is healthy, tell the client which system is failing and who owns it, offer to help them raise it with the vendor as a courtesy or as quoted work, and keep the out-of-scope boundary from the charter intact without leaving them stranded

edge_cases.description: The operator is ill or unreachable for a week and nobody else can access the portfolio
edge_cases.trigger: single-operator unavailability during a live obligation
edge_cases.mitigation: keep a documented emergency arrangement - a trusted contractor with a break-glass path into the vault, the runbooks and the client contact list - state the realistic out-of-hours position in the promise rather than pretending to constant cover, and notify clients when cover is degraded

edge_cases.description: The supplier announces that the plan the whole portfolio sits on is discontinued or repriced sharply, with a deadline
edge_cases.trigger: a supplier plan change that breaks the book's economics or its arrangement
edge_cases.mitigation: run the rehearsed migration path on a pilot site first, schedule the rest in batches with client notice, and if the cost genuinely moves, use the repricing protocol with its plain reason and lower-tier or clean-exit alternatives rather than absorbing it silently until the business is unprofitable

workflow.description: Fix the scheduled work, the on-request work, the out-of-scope list and the three standing principles before any site is enrolled
workflow.gate: the charter names the scheduled and on-request work, the refusals, and the ownership, verifiability and capacity principles

workflow.action: Decide the portfolio hosting architecture and prove one site can leave it
workflow.description: Choose the tenancy and isolation model, record who holds each account, list the supplier features depended on, and export and restore one representative site elsewhere
workflow.artifact: hosting architecture note with dependency list and a completed export-and-restore record
workflow.gate: tenancy, isolation boundary and account holders are documented, and one site has been restored on a different provider with the elapsed time recorded

workflow.action: Stand up the account ownership register and delegated access model
workflow.description: Record every account per client with owner, recovery address, access mechanism and renewal date, correcting anything held in the operator's name that should be the client's
workflow.gate: every client-owned asset shows the client's name and every operator access is a revocable delegated mechanism referenced to the vault

workflow.action: Map personal data and set the retention and deletion rules
workflow.description: Record per site what personal data exists and where copies live, the responsibility split with the client, and the deletion window that retention must respect
workflow.artifact: per-site data map with the responsibility split and retention rule
workflow.gate: every copy location including backups and forwarding inboxes is listed, and every regulatory statement carries the instruction to verify current rules in the applicable jurisdiction

workflow.description: Derive scope, frequency, off-account location and retention per site from change rate, tolerable loss and detection lag, inside the deletion rule just set
workflow.artifact: backup schedule and retention policy per site
workflow.gate: each site has scope, frequency, retention and an off-account copy recorded, and the configuration matches what its tier promises

workflow.action: Run the first restore drill and record the measurement
workflow.description: Restore a real site into a scratch location, time it, walk the result, and log the defects found
workflow.artifact: restore drill log with elapsed time, recovery point and defect list
workflow.gate: a restore has been completed and walked end to end, and any client-facing recovery statement now cites this measurement

workflow.action: Instrument availability, expiries and form delivery
workflow.description: Add external checks, certificate and domain expiry watching, licence renewals and form-delivery verification, then test that alerts arrive
workflow.artifact: monitoring configuration and the portfolio expiry calendar
workflow.gate: every site is externally checked, every expiry has a date, owner and payment instrument, and an alert test reached the operator

workflow.action: Establish the update cycle and the security baseline
workflow.description: Define batch windows with pre-update restore points, the security fast path, the per-site functional walk, the rollback rule, and the hygiene set of vaulted credentials, least-privilege accounts and removal of unused code
workflow.artifact: update and security runbook with the tech-debt log
workflow.gate: one full round has been executed with restore points, functional walks and outcomes recorded, and blocked or deferred updates appear on the tech-debt log with a remediation path

workflow.action: Build the care tiers, the edit allowance and the response promise
workflow.description: Derive tier contents from the procedures that now exist, define the included-edit unit with concrete examples and the rollover rule, and set response windows that survive a bad week
workflow.artifact: tier definition sheet with allowance boundary and response windows
workflow.gate: every tier promise maps to an existing procedure, no tier contains unlimited human work, and the floor obligations are stated as applying to all tiers

workflow.action: Enroll each launched site through the intake checklist
workflow.description: Verify the runbook against the live site, take and verify the first backup, prove delegated access, register expiries, and record tier inclusions and billing terms before the first charge
workflow.gate: no site is in billing without a verified backup and restore point, working access, active monitoring, registered expiries and written tier and cancellation terms

workflow.action: Start the reporting cadence under the claim-integrity rules
workflow.description: Produce the monthly report from operational records, schedule the periodic review conversation, and check every statement against the no-guarantee and evidence-on-request rules
workflow.artifact: monthly report template plus the review-conversation agenda
workflow.gate: each report line reconciles to a record, deferred work and upcoming expiries are disclosed, and no ranking, traffic or revenue promise appears anywhere

workflow.action: Prepare the exit pack, the dunning ladder and the book review cadence
workflow.description: Assemble and test the handover pack on a live site, write the escalation ladder the client agrees at enrollment, and set the cadence for reviewing capacity and every account
workflow.artifact: handover pack template, dunning ladder and book review schedule
workflow.gate: a test handover has been produced end to end, the ladder and suspension terms are the ones clients actually agree to, and nothing in the pack is conditional on payment

dominance_rules.rule: Client asset ownership dominates every retention and collections decision
dominance_rules.rationale: the entire positioning of this business is that clients stay because the service is good, and one hostage situation destroys that positioning permanently in a small local market
dominance_rules.trigger: a balance is owed, a client is leaving, or a departing client asks for their assets during a dispute
dominance_rules.action: release the domain, content, database, backups and credentials on request regardless of the balance, and pursue money through the agreed terms and ordinary collections only

dominance_rules.rule: A verified restore point dominates any update, migration or quick fix
dominance_rules.rationale: everything else in the operation is recoverable if a known-good copy exists, and nothing is if it does not
dominance_rules.trigger: any change to a live site, including an urgent one
dominance_rules.action: take and label a restore point first, or stop until one exists

dominance_rules.rationale: security patching, breach notification, a working backup and an honest incident response are owed to every site under management, and gating them creates both an ethical failure and the portfolio's own infection route
dominance_rules.trigger: a security fix, a notification duty or a recovery need arises on a low-tier account
dominance_rules.action: perform the floor work regardless of tier and address the economics separately through repricing or re-scoping

dominance_rules.rationale: a single unprovable promise made during a renewal conversation outlives every honest report that preceded it
dominance_rules.trigger: any client-facing number, promise or comparison, especially under competitive pressure
dominance_rules.action: state only what a record can evidence, name what is not guaranteed, and refuse ranking, traffic, lead and revenue promises outright

dominance_rules.rule: Ethical constraints dominate saving the account
dominance_rules.rationale: an account retained by frightening or confusing someone is a complaint, a refund and a reputation problem waiting for its trigger
dominance_rules.trigger: a save attempt, a renewal conversation, or an upsell to a client who cannot evaluate the technical claim
dominance_rules.action: restrict the response to facts, a fix, a right-sized tier or a graceful exit, and record confirmed understanding where the client cannot judge the claim

dominance_rules.rationale: promises already sold to existing clients are obligations, while the next sale is only an opportunity
dominance_rules.trigger: a new site is ready to enroll while the recurring hours plus reserve are already consumed
dominance_rules.action: pause enrollment, standardize or trim the book first, and tell the incoming client a realistic start date rather than absorbing the work

dominance_rules.rule: The written tier definition dominates verbal expectation in any inclusion dispute
dominance_rules.rationale: memory is unreliable on both sides and an unresolvable dispute costs more than the work being argued about
dominance_rules.trigger: a client believes something is included that the tier does not list
dominance_rules.action: resolve from the written definition; where the definition is genuinely ambiguous, resolve once in the client's favour and fix the wording for everyone the same week

dominance_rules.rule: Disclosure before an irreversible or billable action dominates convenience
dominance_rules.rationale: surprises in an invoice or a migration destroy more trust than the underlying change ever would
dominance_rules.trigger: a price change, a supplier migration, billable overflow work, or a suspension date approaching
dominance_rules.action: disclose in writing in advance with the reason and the alternatives, and only then act

dominance_rules.rule: Portability dominates margin when an architecture choice would trap a site
dominance_rules.rationale: an exit that cannot be executed cleanly turns the ownership promise into marketing and removes the operator's own freedom to change supplier
dominance_rules.trigger: a supplier feature, format or plan would make a single site unexportable or a migration untestable
dominance_rules.action: decline the feature or add a parallel export path before adopting it, and record the replacement cost of every proprietary dependency taken on

dominance_rules.rule: Facts dominate blame during an incident
dominance_rules.rationale: clients forgive failures they were told about honestly and rarely forgive discovering the truth later or being handed an excuse
dominance_rules.trigger: any outage, compromise or breakage, including one caused by the supplier or by the operator's own mistake
dominance_rules.action: communicate what is known, what is being done and what is unknown, name the operator's own error plainly when it is one, and follow with the post-incident note

anti_rework_rules.rule: Verify a restore on a site before running its first update cycle
anti_rework_rules.prevents: discovering during a real failure that the backup was never valid, which turns a routine rollback into a rebuild

anti_rework_rules.rule: Record account ownership and delegated access at enrollment rather than at exit
anti_rework_rules.prevents: an offboarding scramble that looks like hostage-taking and costs unbillable hours reconstructing who owns what

anti_rework_rules.rule: Set the data map and deletion rule before choosing backup retention windows
anti_rework_rules.prevents: rebuilding the entire backup regime after the first deletion request proves the retention design impossible to honour

anti_rework_rules.rule: Design care tiers only after the procedures they promise exist and their effort is known
anti_rework_rules.prevents: selling promises the operation cannot keep, which is repaid in missed windows, apologies and eventual repricing

anti_rework_rules.rule: Agree the single request channel, the included-edit examples and the response windows before the first request arrives
anti_rework_rules.prevents: months of scattered unlogged work that cannot be counted, reported, billed or used in cost measurement

anti_rework_rules.rule: Put monitoring and the expiry calendar in place before the first renewal season
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a lapsed domain or expired certificate emergency that costs a weekend, a client's trust and sometimes the domain itself

anti_rework_rules.rule: Measure cost-to-serve from logged minutes before touching any price
anti_rework_rules.prevents: repricing by feel, which typically raises prices on the accounts that are already profitable and keeps the ones consuming the book

anti_rework_rules.rule: Test the handover pack on a live site before the first real exit
anti_rework_rules.prevents: the first genuine departure becoming the discovery that the export is incomplete, in front of the client and their new provider

anti_rework_rules.rule: Write the incident communication template before an incident happens
anti_rework_rules.prevents: improvised messages written under pressure that over-promise a fix time, blame a supplier, or say nothing at all until the client finds out elsewhere

anti_rework_rules.rule: Standardize the stack and the schedule across the portfolio before growing the book
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a collection of per-site snowflakes that makes every batch operation impossible and every capacity estimate wrong

iteration_protocol.trigger: a restore drill fails or takes materially longer than the recovery time clients were told
iteration_protocol.action: fix the defect in the backup regime, re-run the drill on that site, and correct every client-facing recovery statement to the new measurement

iteration_protocol.trigger: an incident occurs, of any cause including the operator's own error
iteration_protocol.action: run the post-incident note and apply its one procedure change to the update, security or monitoring runbook before the next window

iteration_protocol.trigger: measured cost-to-serve exceeds a tier's assumption for consecutive periods on the same account
iteration_protocol.action: work the ladder in order - find and fix the cause, then re-scope the tier, and only then start the repricing protocol with notice and alternatives

iteration_protocol.trigger: cancellation reasons cluster around one promise, one tier or one segment of the book
iteration_protocol.action: diagnose which promise is actually failing and repair the operation or the tier definition before offering any discount

iteration_protocol.trigger: the supplier changes pricing, terms or ownership, or deprecates the plan the portfolio uses
iteration_protocol.action: re-run the dependency and exit assessment, pilot the migration path on one site, and decide on the written switch triggers rather than in the moment

iteration_protocol.trigger: a platform version or a widely used extension reaches end of life or is abandoned
iteration_protocol.action: list the affected portfolio slice, disclose the blocked updates in those clients' reports, and sequence rebuild or replacement conversations before the security position becomes indefensible

iteration_protocol.trigger: operational windows, drills or reports start slipping, or response windows are missed more than rarely
iteration_protocol.action: treat it as a capacity signal - pause enrollment, run the account-by-account review, standardize outliers and release or right-size the accounts consuming the reserve

iteration_protocol.trigger: a client says the monthly report tells them nothing, or reports go unopened across the book
iteration_protocol.action: rewrite the report around specific work and upcoming decisions for that site, add the review conversation where it is missing, and keep every added line traceable to a record

priority_rationale: The charter comes first because every tier, checklist, report and exit pack is derived from the promise set and its standing principles; hosting architecture, supplier exit and the ownership register follow because they fix containment, portability and who owns what before any site is taken on; enrollment intake then gates sites into operations, where backups, proven restores, updates, security, monitoring and incident response are built in that order because each is the precondition of the next and none of them may be promised before they exist; tier design, the edit boundary, the response promise and cost-to-serve come after operations because a tier can only sell demonstrated capability; reporting and claim integrity follow because they publish what operations did under rules that keep every statement verifiable; and churn triage, dunning, ethical guardrails, reactivation, capacity review and offboarding come last because they manage the book that all the preceding work has made worth keeping - and because the exit, executed cleanly with everything handed back, is what makes the whole retention model honest.
